Yes. Downtime has to be measured in minutes, from the stop until the first good part, and tied to a reason code—not just a technician’s free-text comment. I also need the repair history to show who did the work and when, so the records hold up over time.

The outgoing technician updates the work order with the machine condition, isolation status, parts used, tests completed, and what remains to be done, then discusses it with the incoming shift lead. In practice, the verbal handoff is more reliable than the paperwork, and that creates gaps when someone is absent or the repair changes during the shift. I need the open repair and its next action to be immediately visible by machine and shift.

Yes. A night-shift repair on Molder 8 was left showing “awaiting parts,” but the technician had actually installed a temporary seal and was waiting for a pressure test; the day shift didn’t know that and started troubleshooting from the beginning. We lost nearly an hour because the work order didn’t show the temporary repair or the next required test.

Lockout/tagout means isolating every hazardous-energy source, applying a personal lock and tag, and verifying zero energy before work starts. The record has to identify who performed the lockout, the date and time it was applied, and who authorized and performed the release; we retain that for regulatory inspections.

It needs the equipment ID, location, problem and sensor evidence, hazard assessment, corrective action, inspection findings, and the names and timestamps of everyone who stopped, worked on, verified, and released the equipment. I also need the lockout/tagout record attached, with a clear history of changes so nobody can quietly overwrite a safety-critical entry, and it must be easy to retrieve as one complete record during an inspection.

You’ve got the general direction, but you missed a few safety-critical pieces. The record must preserve the full lockout/tagout history, including who applied and released each lock and when; near misses must be reported within 24 hours; and any chemical spill needs its own environmental report. Also, the system must capture verification that work stopped and the equipment was made safe, without distracting operators around moving machinery.

Energy sources are anything that can injure someone if they aren’t isolated—electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, mechanical, thermal, chemical, or stored energy such as pressure or gravity. Before maintenance, the technician identifies every source, isolates it, locks and tags it, and verifies zero energy before touching the equipment.

The record needs the equipment and job identified, every energy source listed, the isolation steps completed, and zero-energy verification recorded. It must show who applied each lock and tag, when it was applied, who verified the isolation, and who released it when the work was complete. A supervisor also needs to review it before the job is closed, and incomplete fields must prevent closeout rather than being left for the next shift.

I mentioned the machine release decision—the record must show who approved putting it back into production and when. For safety-related parts, that approval is part of the repair traceability, not an optional note.

The maintenance technician enters the work order and corrective-action details, while the shift supervisor validates the hazard controls before closeout. Safety-critical records, including isolation status and return-to-service authorization, must be updated before equipment release, not at the end of the shift.

A required digital handoff with the critical fields completed and acknowledged by the incoming supervisor would help most. No equipment gets released while isolation status, alarms, permits, and unresolved hazards are blank.
